frames.narration: A maintainer's CI publishes webkit 2.2.0. It proves its identity with a short-lived OIDC token from the registered repository and workflow, and sends the tarball with a signed statement of the source commit and builder.

The identity is accepted, so the registry API hashes the tarball with SHA-256 and checks that webkit 2.2.0 does not exist yet. A version can be written only once. The attestation is added to the public signature log.

The tarball is saved under its hash, and the new version waits in the scanner before it is released. The scanner compares it with 2.1.0 and runs it in a sandbox. It finds no network calls or install scripts that are new.

The scan passes, so the release goes on the publish queue. The indexer adds 2.2.0 to the webkit metadata document and purges that one URL in the CDN. The version is visible about a minute after the publish started.

Later a developer runs an install with the range ^2.0.0. The client asks the CDN for the webkit metadata document. The CDN had it purged, so it fetches the new one from the index once and then serves everyone.

The client resolves the ranges itself with no more requests to the registry: the highest version that fits ^2.0.0 is 2.2.0. Then it downloads the tarball by its URL, which names the hash, so the CDN can keep it for a year.

The client hashes what it received and compares it with the hash in the metadata, and the signature log shows the build came from the registered repository. It matches, so the package is installed and the hash is written to the lockfile.

Another day, an attacker with a stolen token publishes webkit 2.2.1 with a hidden install script. It has no valid provenance, and the scanner sees a new network call and a credential read. The version is held and never reaches the index, so no build can pick it up.
